content: Animal studies conducted across various species have demonstrated that skin exposure to isocyanates, followed by inhalational challenges, is highly effective in inducing asthmatic lung responses. Human studies, though more limited in scope, suggest a similar mechanism following skin exposure to certain sensitizing chemicals. Despite reductions in inhalational exposure to isocyanates and beryllium in occupational settings, immune-mediated respiratory diseases associated with these compounds continue to occur, often in environments where skin exposure is possible. Collectively, data from both human and animal studies indicate that skin contact with specific chemical allergens may contribute to the development of immune-mediated respiratory diseases, such as asthma or chronic beryllium disease. In laboratory testing, chemical allergens are primarily identified in vivo using traditional guinea pig sensitization tests or the more advanced murine local lymph node assay (LLNA). Relevant data for determining whether a chemical may elicit an immune-mediated response include analytical or descriptive epidemiologic studies, observational case reports from health surveillance programs or poison control centers, and clinical studies. It is important to note that the primary purpose of clinical tests involving human volunteers is to confirm the safety of test materials or preparations, rather than to identify skin sensitization hazards. The SEN notation is assigned when one or more of the following criteria are met: credible evidence indicates the occurrence of allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) or sensitization due to chemical exposure of the skin. Skin sensitization among workers is often clinically characterized by immunologically mediated cutaneous reactions, such as pruritus, erythema, edema, papules, vesicles, bullae, or a combination of these findings. Information from patch testing or antigen-specific immune responses, such as antibody responses or lymphocyte proliferation, is also considered when assigning skin notations. Confirmed case reports describing multiple subjects in more than one independent study, as well as epidemiologic evidence establishing a causal relationship between exposure and sensitization, are critical. When isolated episodes of ACD are observed, supporting evidence, including data from animal tests and structure-activity relationship (SAR) analyses, should be obtained before recognizing the chemical as a contact allergen. Animal data indicating the potential for ACD or other immune-mediated responses associated with skin exposure include guinea pig sensitization tests, LLNA, mouse ear swelling tests, and relevant animal models of asthma. Appendix A outlines protocols and criteria that can be used in assigning the SEN notation. Scientific data beyond those previously described may also be used to demonstrate sensitization resulting from skin exposure to a chemical. For example, research protocols introduced in Appendix A, with variations in evaluation procedures or study designs examining health endpoints other than those evaluated by standardized protocols, may be utilized. An example includes studies evaluating the induction of antigen-mediated responses following skin exposure. When no empirical data of acceptable quality exist, the occurrence of ACD or other immune-mediated responses due to skin exposure to a chemical can be inferred using SAR-based analyses and other computational techniques as alternative methods for hazard identification. An example of SAR analysis is the use of the knowledge-based expert system, Deductive Estimation of Risk from Existing Knowledge (DEREK™), to evaluate the relationship between the molecular structure of a chemical and its allergenic properties. Appendix C describes the DEREK™ expert system for identifying sensitizers. When the algorithm is used as the basis for identification, a positive result is sufficient to classify a chemical as an agent capable of provoking ACD or sensitization from skin exposure and to assign the SEN notation.
